headline: Peconic porgies stack thick at Shelter Island while bass slide into the deep channels
subhead: The bay's shifted into its full summer rhythm — scup biting steady on the reefs, fluke holding the drop-offs, bass working the edges at first light.
body_markdown:
By mid-July the Peconic has settled into the pattern I wait for every year — the water's held in the low-to-mid 70s for weeks now, the bay warmed a good ten days ahead of the Sound like it always does, and the fish have sorted themselves out accordingly. This is the stretch where the bay stops being about who showed up first and starts being about who's willing to fish the right piece of structure at the right minute of the tide. Right now that means porgies on the reefs, fluke in the channels, and bass that have gone crepuscular on you — dawn and dusk, or don't bother.

Start with the scup, because that's been the most dependable thing in this whole system. Shelter Island's rock piles — Cedar Island, the reef off Jenny's Island, the rubble around Bug Light — are holding porgies thick enough that a slow afternoon still puts two dozen keepers in the cooler if you're anchored right. Sandworms and clam strips on a simple two-hook bottom rig, small hooks, light enough sinker to feel the tap-tap before you set. The bite's best on the last two hours of the incoming and the first hour of the outgoing — that window when the current's moving enough to stir bait off bottom but hasn't gone to rip stage yet. I've had my best days anchored up-current of the structure and letting the scent trail work down over the rocks rather than dropping right on top of the pile. Fish are there most of the day, but the bite window is real — miss the tide change and you're just soaking bait for an hour waiting for the next push.

Fluke have settled into their summer address — the channels. Plum Gut's the obvious one and it's producing, but you need to respect that current; it rips through there on a big tide and you'll be dragging bucktails at an angle instead of bouncing them clean. The more forgiving fishing has been in the Shelter Island ferry channels and out toward Noyack, working 20 to 35 feet of water with white Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails, tipped with a strip of squid. Slow drift, bounce it off bottom, let it sit a beat before the next lift — fluke this time of year want it presented slow, not ripped. Sizes have been mixed — plenty of shorts mixed with keepers to 4 and 5 pounds, so you're sorting fish, but that's normal for July. The better keeper ratio has come on the last two hours of the ebb, when bait gets pulled off the flats and funneled through the deeper cuts.

Bass are the honest disappointment if you're expecting the spring pattern to hold — it doesn't, not in mid-July. The bay's warmed past their comfort range through the middle of the day, so they've pushed into the channels and deeper holes and only come up on the edges to feed in low light. Orient Point and the Gut are still your best bets, but I'd be there before the sun's fully up, working a 1.5-ounce bucktail across the current seam and letting it sink clean off the edge before working it back with a slow bottom retrieve — same idea that's been paying off out at Montauk on the bigger fish, and it translates fine to Plum Gut's current edges. Evening's been better than morning some nights, especially on a dropping tide when bait gets pulled out of Gardiners Bay past Orient. Don't expect steady action — it's been more of a bite-or-nothing proposition, a handful of solid fish in a short window rather than a stretch you can fish for three hours straight.

Bluefish have been the wild card — when they show, they show hard, chopping bait on the surface off Orient and out toward Plum Gut, and a bucktail or a Hopkins worked fast through the melee will get bit instantly. But they're not consistent yet this week; some days the birds are working and some days the bay's dead calm with nothing showing.

Weakfish are still around in small numbers — Three Mile Harbor and the deeper holes off Sag Harbor have given up a few on soft plastics fished slow along bottom at dusk, but I wouldn't plan a trip around them. They're a bonus, not a target, the way they've been for a few years now in this bay.

Looking ahead, I don't see much reason for the pattern to break. The bay's thermal structure is locked in for summer — warm shallows during the day, bass and bluefish pushed to channel edges and low-light windows, porgies steady on the reefs regardless of what the sun's doing. If the wind stays out of the south and lays down through the week, I'd fish the Shelter Island reefs midday for porgies and be at Plum Gut or Orient for the last hour of light chasing bass and blues. That's the two-tide day that's been working, and until something shifts — a cold push, a big blow that stirs the bay — I don't expect the rhythm to change much.
